questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The temple plan as a diagram of belief
questions.learningObjective: read a temple plan as an ordering of approach rather than as a structural diagram
questions.stem: A visitor climbs the steps of a Greek temple, walks between the outer columns, and comes to face a closed inner room that cannot be entered. What does that sequence of spaces express?

options.text: A hierarchy of approach, since the colonnade and the inner room set ordered stages before the thing that is kept closed
The builder's convenience, since a column grid on a rectangular plan is simply the easiest way to roof a room
options.misconception: reads the plan as construction convenience instead of as an ordering of approach and access

options.text: A water scheme, since the steps around the building are shaped to carry rainwater away from the foundations
options.misconception: takes the raised platform for a drainage channel rather than for the base the columns stand on

options.text: A record of rebuilds, since the number of columns on the plan counts how often the site was cleared and rebuilt
options.misconception: believes the column count records rebuilding rather than setting proportion and symmetry

questions.explanation: The plan is a sequence and a sequence is an argument. The visitor is made to leave ordinary ground, climb, cross a threshold, and pass a colonnade that frames whatever lies behind it, and only then face the closed room; each stage narrows the possibility of acting, and that narrowing is the content of the building. The closed inner room is not an unfinished or excluded space but the point of the arrangement, kept shut precisely so that it is faced rather than entered, and the outer columns are what turn a plain box into something that is presented. A reading that calls the grid merely convenient has taken the part that is easy to explain and discarded the part that is hard. The steps are the base the columns stand on, and while water is indeed thrown clear of a foundation, that is what any raised platform does. As for the column count, the regular peristyle sets the proportions of the whole; a difference in the numbers between one temple and another is evidence about date and design, not a tally of clearing episodes.
questions.hint: Ask what the visitor is prevented from doing, and at which point in the walk the building prevents it.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Reading a described temple plan
questions.learningObjective: infer the sequence of a building from a described plan
questions.stem: A plan is described as follows: a low platform of three steps, a colonnade running the full length of two long sides, an entrance porch at one end, a single undivided room behind it, and a rear porch with no door. What is this arrangement doing?

options.text: It stages an approach, admitting the visitor to the enclosure but not to the room, and the closed rear confirms that the route ends there
It records a rebuilding, since a porch without a door shows the building was left unfinished at the point of collapse
options.misconception: reads an unglazed rear porch as abandoned work rather than as a closed end

options.text: It is a warehouse plan, since a single undivided room with a porch at each end is the standard arrangement for storing goods
options.misconception: assumes a single undivided room indicates storage, ignoring the entrance sequence

options.text: It is a defensive plan, since the colonnade of two long sides gives a protected wall along the approach and the ends
options.misconception: supplies a military function for a colonnade that frames rather than shields

questions.explanation: Each element of the description does work only in sequence. The three steps lift the visitor off ordinary ground, the colonnade on the two long sides means the approach is flanked rather than exposed, the front porch gives a defined entrance, and the single undivided room is the destination that is nonetheless not entered. The rear porch without a door is the decisive detail: it is built, roofed and finished, so the building is not unfinished, but it is not an exit either, and that is what fixes the direction of the whole route. Read that way the plan is a piece of control. A storage building would be entered directly rather than approached, and a defensive plan would thicken its edges and close its openings, which a colonnade of slender columns does the opposite of.
questions.hint: Ask why the rear porch was built at all if no door was ever cut into the room behind it.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The column grid of a hypostyle hall
questions.learningObjective: state what a repeated column grid carries and what it costs the interior
questions.stem: A hypostyle hall is described as a forest of stone columns carrying architraves and a roof over a wide room. What follows from building the roof that way?

options.text: The roof can span a great width only along the short direction of each bay, so the hall fills with rows of repeated supports
The hall can be cleared of its columns in one move, since a repeated grid is only a diagram and carries no weight at all
options.misconception: believes a column grid is a diagram, when the columns carry the load

options.text: The stone columns can be slimmer than they would be as walls, since a column is always the more economical of the two
options.misconception: assumes a column is structurally more efficient than a wall, ignoring the load it must carry

options.text: The roof becomes lighter, since splitting a load across many columns reduces the weight each one takes
options.misconception: supposes many small supports lighten a structure, though the total weight is unchanged

questions.explanation: Before the arch and the truss, a horizontal member of stone can only be carried at its two ends, and a stone beam has to be deep and short to survive its own weight. So the span between supports has a limit, and a wide roof is achieved by placing supports at intervals rather than by making the members longer. Repeat that interval across a wide room and you get rows, which is what a hypostyle hall is: many columns, a regular grid, and a clear height set by the architrave and everything above it. The cost is interior space, since the columns occupy the floor the room was for, and that cost was accepted because the alternative was a wall across the width. A column is not slimmer than a wall for free, either: it carries a concentrated load in bending, and the shaft is sized to do exactly that.
questions.hint: Ask how far a horizontal stone member can reach unaided, and what that limit forces into the middle of the room.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The thrust a masonry arch contains
questions.learningObjective: explain how an arch turns a vertical load into a lateral push
questions.stem: A semicircular arch of wedge-shaped stones carries a wall above it. Why do the stones stay in place, and what does the arch do to the load?

options.text: The wedge shapes lock against each other in compression and pass the weight sideways into the supports at each springing
The central stone is in tension and pulls the rest of the arch together, holding it up like a tightened rope
options.misconception: treats the keystone as a tension member, when masonry works in compression

options.text: The stones are held by the friction of their weight alone, so an arch is really a tall stack with gaps bridged at the top
options.misconception: attributes an arch to friction alone and denies the geometry of the ring

options.text: The arch keeps the load travelling straight down each stone, so the wall above needs no support until the arch is fully closed
options.misconception: supposes the arch carries load straight down rather than pressing outwards

questions.explanation: Cut every arch stone as a wedge and the assembly gains a property no stack of blocks has: as the wedges are brought together, each presses on its neighbours, and the ring closes into a single compressive object. Stone is enormously strong in compression and hopeless in tension, so this is the direction masonry wants, and the arch exploits it exactly. What it cannot do is send the load straight down. The weight of the wall above passes from stone to stone around the curve and arrives at the springings, where it has become a sideways push, and the arch is only stable if something on each side takes that push. That is why the buttress or pier beside a vaulted opening is not decoration or support for the wall above but part of the arch itself. The keystone closes the ring and is the last stone placed; it is in compression like all the rest, and the arch is held by geometry, not by a rope.
questions.hint: Ask which direction masonry is strong in, and where a sideways push has to be caught.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The load path of a barrel vault
questions.learningObjective: trace the load path of a barrel vault to its buttresses
questions.stem: A barrel vault is a tunnel of masonry built over a long hall, and heavy buttresses stand along the side walls at intervals. What are the buttresses for?

options.text: They resist the sideways push the vault throws at each springing, and they are spaced with the bays for that reason
They carry the roof timbers, since the vault is too light to take the weight of the structure above it
options.misconception: assigns buttresses to the roof, ignoring the lateral thrust the vault makes

options.text: They raise the wall so the vault can be built at a greater height above the ground of the hall
options.misconception: thinks a buttress adds height to the wall rather than resisting the vault

options.text: They hold the ends of the vault shut, preventing the barrel from opening out at the two gable ends
options.misconception: locates the thrust at the vault ends, when it arrives at the springings along the sides

questions.explanation: A barrel vault is one arch extended along its length, so the lateral push that any single arch makes at its springings is repeated at every point down that length. Concentrating the whole thrust at two ends is impossible, and the practical answer is to build a buttress opposite each bay and let the mass of the masonry take the push back into the ground. That is why buttresses on a vaulted hall are not scattered at random: their rhythm follows the bays, because the bays are the units of vaulting and the buttresses are the units of resistance. A buttress that does not correspond to a bay is wasting mass, and a bay whose springing has no buttress in front of it is a bay that will open at the joint. The wall above the springing also tells you which way the load runs, since it is carried directly down the pier and thickened where the vault arrives.
questions.hint: Ask how often a barrel vault throws its push sideways, and what would happen along the wall if nothing met it.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A free arch span with no buttress behind it
questions.learningObjective: read a described arch as a load-path claim
questions.stem: A long arcade of semicircular arches is described as standing free, with the wall above carried on columns and no mass of masonry at any springing except the columns themselves. What is the structural claim being made?

options.text: That the arches span between columns and depend on the column bases for the lateral push, which is why the columns are heavy and closely spaced
That the arches carry their own weight straight down into the pavement, so the columns serve only as an upright frame
options.misconception: believes the arch delivers a vertical load and treats the columns as non-structural

options.text: That the wall above is a light infill resting on the arches and adds nothing to the load they carry
options.misconception: treats a wall above a vault as an inert infill rather than as load

options.text: That the arcade is unfinished, since a complete arcade would have a continuous wall at the piers to take the thrust
options.misconception: calls a free arcade incomplete when the absence of a wall is the design

questions.explanation: Nothing in masonry can be allowed to push outward unchecked, so an arch that has no wall beside it must be given the mass it needs in the members that receive the push. Here those members are the columns: they are spaced closely so that the span between them is small, they are made broad in the direction of the thrust so the compression spreads, and their bases are wide enough to distribute the remaining force into the ground. The free-standing arcade is a considered answer to the problem, not a gap in the design, and the heaviness of the supports is exactly the evidence of the thrust being taken there. The wall above is not inert; a spandrel wall adds its own weight at the haunches, which is precisely where an arch carries the greatest load. A free arcade in masonry is expensive in mass, and that expense is the price of not needing a buttress.
questions.hint: Ask where the sideways push goes when there is no wall on either side of the arch.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Where a groin vault concentrates its load
questions.learningObjective: explain why a groin vault pushes at its four corners
questions.stem: A groin vault is made where two barrel vaults cross at right angles, and it covers a square bay instead of a corridor. What changes about the load compared with a barrel vault?

options.text: The two barrels no longer push along the whole length, so the thrust is gathered at four corners and those piers carry it
Nothing changes, since crossing two barrels simply doubles the thrust and a groin vault therefore needs twice the buttressing
options.misconception: thinks crossing vaults doubles the thrust instead of concentrating it at four points

options.text: The load drops straight into the four corners, so the vault no longer throws any sideways push at all
options.misconception: denies lateral thrust in a groin vault, when the corners resist it

options.text: The walls become free of load, since the cross vaults span corner to corner and touch the side walls at the crown only
options.misconception: believes a groin vault relieves the side walls rather than concentrating force at the corners

questions.explanation: The advantage of the cross is that the barrels no longer run the whole length of the space. Each one is cut off at the diagonal, so instead of a continuous thrust along two long walls the vault delivers its force along the four diagonals, and those diagonals arrive at the four corners. The architect's opportunity is that four corner piers can carry the whole bay, and the walls between them are relieved; the cost is that those four piers must be heavy and that the geometry of the transition from a square bay to a circle has to be solved. This is why a church built with groin vaults is structurally legible in a way a barrel-vaulted hall is not: you can see where the forces go. Saying the thrust doubles ignores the interruption, and saying the thrust disappears is precisely what the corner piers exist to prevent.
questions.hint: Ask where a barrel vault would push, and then ask what happens when the barrel is stopped short at a corner.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Squinches and pendentives as a geometric transition
questions.learningObjective: state the problem a squinch or pendentive solves
questions.stem: A dome needs a circular base to spring from, but the bay beneath it is square with four corner piers. What are squinches and pendentives for?

options.text: They bridge the square bay to the circle above, so the dome has a continuous round base to spring from
They thicken the walls so the piers can take the extra weight the dome adds to the corners of the bay
options.misconception: treats them as extra mass for the load rather than as a shape for the base

options.text: They close the upper part of the bay so the dome cannot be seen from the floor of the building at all
options.misconception: supposes they conceal the dome instead of supporting its circular base

options.text: They carry a walkway around the top of the bay from which the dome could be repaired and inspected
options.misconception: reads them as a maintenance gallery rather than as a structural transition

questions.explanation: This is a geometry problem before it is an engineering one. A dome is generated by rotating a curve about a vertical axis, so it needs a circle to sit on, and a square bay with four corner piers offers four corners and four straight sides. Something has to occupy the difference between those two shapes, and there are two classical ways. A squinch does it with masonry: arches are built across the corners, one over another, until the space is a small square rotated to stand on a corner, which can then be inscribed in the circle. A pendentive does it with a curved triangle: a segment of the sphere is carved as a spherical triangle whose base is the pier and whose apex is the full height of the bay, so four of them together make the continuous concave surface a dome springs from. Both are described by their shape, and both are visible as surface, which is why they are also the place where a builder puts ornament.
questions.hint: Ask what shape a dome needs to stand on, and what the bay beneath it actually offers.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The geometry that closes a dome
questions.learningObjective: describe how a hemisphere is divided into a buildable shell
questions.stem: A masonry dome is built up in horizontal courses that narrow towards the top. What geometric fact lets a builder close the top at all?

options.text: The courses are wedges in a circle, so they meet at a point, and they lock in compression exactly as arch stones do
The top can be closed with a single flat stone, since the courses above it are light enough to need no support
options.misconception: assumes the courses near the crown carry no load, when they carry the least and the ring needs most care

options.text: The dome is closed by a timber roof above it, which keeps the masonry courses from having to meet at all
options.misconception: supplies a timber closure where the masonry ring itself closes

options.text: The courses are mortared at the crown, and the mortar's grip is what holds the two halves of the dome together
options.misconception: credits mortar adhesion for the stability that the ring of wedges provides

questions.explanation: Look at a dome in plan and the whole thing is a set of circles, one inside another, each a course. A course is a ring of wedge-shaped blocks whose joints radiate from the crown, so every course is an arch turned on its side, and the assembly works by the same principle as a masonry arch: compression and a lock. Because the radius shrinks towards the top, each course sits partly inside the one below, which lets the shell stand while the masons leave the scaffolding they are working from. The crown is closed by a small plate or stone set over the final ring, and the difficulty is entirely in the courses below it, where the ring is at its heaviest and the weight of everything above bears down. A flat stone is what closes the top, not what holds it, and mortar is a bedding material, not a structural adhesive in this arrangement.
questions.hint: Ask what one course of a dome is in plan, and how many arches' worth of behaviour that gives.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The hoop push at the foot of a dome
questions.learningObjective: explain the outward push at the base of a dome and what resists it
questions.stem: A hemispherical dome is described as resting on a ring of piers, and heavy metal bands are set into the masonry where the dome meets its base. What problem are the bands answering?

options.text: The shell wants to spread sideways at its foot like a hoop, and the ring of masonry and its metal ties resist that spreading
The dome is too light to load the piers, so the bands add weight and keep the shell from lifting off at the crown
options.misconception: supposes metal bands are ballast against uplift rather than ties against spread

options.text: The bands stop rainwater entering the joints where the dome meets the wall of the drum below it
options.misconception: reads a metal tie as waterproofing at the springing

options.text: The bands let the masons cut the dome in more courses than the geometry allows, since each course is clamped by the one above
options.misconception: supposes metal ties compensate for courses the geometry should have fixed

questions.explanation: A dome is a curved shell and a curved shell behaves like a hoop. Under its own weight it develops a thrust around the base that tries to open the ring outward, and because the ring is in compression it cannot simply expand. A low, heavy ring of masonry around the foot is the first line of resistance, since its own weight resists being pushed apart; where that is not enough, metal ties are set into the masonry, and they work in tension, which is a material masonry cannot supply. A row of old cannon or a lead casing was often used because a material that cannot take a squeeze will take a pull. The crown does not lift, so uplift is not the problem being solved, and water is a conservation problem handled by drainage, not by a band buried in the stonework. This is the same physics as a barrel arch, wrapped round a circle.
questions.hint: Ask what a curved shell does to its own edge, and which material can pull when stone cannot.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a drum under a dome buys
questions.learningObjective: explain the two functions of a drum beneath a dome
questions.stem: A large dome is described as resting on a tall cylindrical wall pierced with rings of windows, with the arch of the dome springing well above the heads of the people below. What does the drum do?

options.text: It lifts the springing clear of the room so the whole opening can be seen from inside, and its thickness gives the dome a continuous base
It shortens the dome's rise, since the drum takes up the height and lets the shell be flatter without losing span
options.misconception: believes the drum flattens the shell rather than raising where it begins

options.text: It reduces the weight the dome carries by holding water and fittings outside the shell rather than inside it
options.misconception: supposes a drum lightens a dome instead of carrying and supporting it

options.text: It lets the builders skip the transition from a square bay to a circle, since the drum is round and needs no pendentives
options.misconception: thinks a round drum removes the need for the square-to-circle transition

questions.explanation: Two problems, two answers. The first is a problem of the eye. If a dome springs from a low ring, the curve begins inside the room and a person standing below sees only a slice of the ceiling, because the shell is already closing overhead. Raise the springing on a drum and the underside of the whole dome lifts into view at once, which is why the famous interiors built this way read as a single continuous surface above the worshippers rather than as a lid. The second is a problem of the base: a dome needs a continuous circular support, and a drum of thick masonry supplies exactly that, distributing the load of the shell into the piers below. The drum cannot be thin, and a ring of windows in it has to be set deep enough to carry the thrust, which is why those openings look small from outside and generous from within. The square-to-circle transition is still needed at the level below the drum, not above it.
questions.hint: Ask what a person standing underneath can see when the springing is low, and what shape the shell needs to sit on.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A drum described as a ring of piers
questions.learningObjective: read a described drum as a load-distributing element
questions.stem: A drum beneath a dome is described as built not of solid wall but of forty closely spaced piers connected by arches, with the dome's weight arriving through a continuous ring above them. What follows from that construction?

options.text: The ring of masonry above can spread the dome's load along its whole length, so the piers each receive a share rather than the full weight at one point
The drum is lighter than a solid wall, so the dome's load is reduced and the piers can be slender without any loss of strength
options.misconception: confuses a lighter drum with a smaller load, which is a separate question

options.text: The piers act as a colonnade, since the dome's weight is carried by their shafts alone and the connecting arches are decorative
options.misconception: dismisses the connecting arches, which are what tie the piers into one ring

options.text: The windows through the piers are structural, since a pierced drum can only stand because the openings stiffen the wall
options.misconception: reverses the relation, claiming openings add stiffness rather than removing material

questions.explanation: Look at where the load is stated to arrive and the purpose of the construction follows. A dome does not press on a few points; it delivers a ring of compression, continuous around the base, and a continuous ring of masonry is an excellent distributor because it can share a force sideways along its length. Below it, forty piers each take a fraction of the total rather than a quarter of it, and that is what allows the wall to be pierced for light without a fatal loss of section. The drum being lighter than solid wall is a separate and much smaller fact, and it does not reduce the load the shell delivers. Nor are the arches between the piers decoration: they are what stops forty separate shafts from behaving as forty separate columns, and they tie the ring together under the outward push. Openings remove material, and a wall stands because of the material left in it.
questions.hint: Ask what shape the dome delivers its weight in, and what a continuous ring can do that separate piers cannot.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The vertical function of a bell tower
questions.learningObjective: state the acoustic and civic function of a bell tower
questions.stem: A bell tower stands apart from the church it belongs to, tall and hollow, with openings near the top. Why is it built so high?

options.text: Height lifts the sound free of the buildings around it, and the openings let it out instead of holding it inside the shaft
Height is decorative, so the tower is a visible marker placed where it can be seen against the skyline
options.misconception: reduces the tower to appearance when its first function is acoustic

options.text: Height lets the bells be hoisted higher, so fewer people have to climb to reach them when they are rung
options.misconception: treats the height as a labour-saving device for the bell keepers

options.text: Height adds mass to the wall, which is what the vault of the church needs as a buttress to take its thrust
options.misconception: makes the tower a buttress, a role the separated shaft does not perform

questions.explanation: Two facts explain the form, and they are both about sound. The first is that a bell's voice carries: the useful thing about a tower is not that the bell is high up but that the sound is released into open air instead of into a roofed room, which is why the belfry is a chamber of openings near the top with the bell hung inside it. The second is that a tower tells you where a church is and what time it is, which is a civic service, and a tower sited apart from the church body can be heard from streets the church itself does not reach. That is also why the tower is built as a hollow shaft rather than a solid pier: a solid shaft would carry the weight and contribute nothing to the sound. Marking the skyline is a real effect of the height, but it is a consequence; the openings and the release of the sound are the reason.
questions.hint: Ask what the openings near the top are for, and what would happen if the shaft were solid.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A described belfry opening
questions.learningObjective: read a described belfry opening as an acoustic decision
questions.stem: The top stage of a bell tower is described as having one tall opening on each side, cut far deeper than the wall is thick, with the bell hung inside a timber frame that does not touch the masonry. What is the design doing?

options.text: Giving the bell an unobstructed way out in two directions and isolating the frame, so the sound is not damped by contact with the wall
Cutting the wall thin so the tower weighs less and the bells can be lifted into the stage more easily than before
options.misconception: reads the deep opening as a weight-saving cut rather than an acoustic provision

options.text: Reducing the top stage to a frame so the tower reads as a lantern against the sky rather than as a solid mass
options.misconception: treats the open stage as a visual effect rather than a working belfry

options.text: Blocking rain from the bell chamber, since an opening left open at the top would let water into the tower
options.misconception: supposes the opening is weather protection, when it is the reverse

questions.explanation: A bell is a sound source and a suspended frame is its resonator, so the arrangement around it is a small piece of instrument design. The deep opening is not a window but an exit: cut deeply, it gives the voice a free path out without the stonework in front of it absorbing and scattering what comes through, which is why belfry stages with shallow arched holes sound muffled by comparison. One opening on each side means the sound leaves on two axes, so it carries in more than one direction across a town. As for the frame, hanging the bell so it does not touch the masonry is deliberate: a bell fixed into the wall loses its resonance into the stone, and the ringing stops carrying. Rain is a real problem for bells and roofs, which is why the top is covered; that is a reason for a roof over the stage, not for closing its sides.
questions.hint: Ask where a bell's sound goes if the frame is bolted to the stone, and what a deep opening avoids on the way out.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The circulation of a cloister
questions.learningObjective: explain the route a cloister organises
questions.stem: A cloister is described as a covered walk running round four sides of an open court, with an arcade facing the court and a wall of the church along one side. What does the route allow?

options.text: Continuous walking beside the court, so processions and daily movement can pass the church wall without going outside
Direct entry to the church from every side, since the arcade is opened wherever the processions need to pass
options.misconception: believes the arcade opens into the church, when the wall blocks it

options.text: A single approach on one axis only, since the walk is designed to reach one door and then stop at it
options.misconception: supplies one axis for a circuit that is continuous and closed

options.text: Unroofed movement between the buildings, since a covered walk would keep the monks from seeing the court they walk around
options.misconception: treats a roof as a barrier to sight, when the court stays fully visible

questions.explanation: The cloister is a circulation device before it is anything else. It gives a covered route that runs right round an open court, which means a procession can move continuously without leaving the precinct, and it can do so in poor weather and in any season. One side is the church wall, so the circuit is also the processional approach: the congregation walks beside the wall and arrives at the door already gathered and in order. The arcade is a feature of the court side, where it opens to the light and to the garden, not a set of doors into the church. And because the walk is a circuit, it also distributes: from anywhere on it you can reach the chapter house, the refectory, the cloister of the novices, without crossing an open yard. It is urbanism at monastic scale.
questions.hint: Ask what a continuous covered route lets a community do that a straight path would not.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The open court inside a cloister
questions.learningObjective: explain what the cloister garth was for
questions.stem: The court at the centre of a cloister is described as a square of open ground, often planted, with a well or a tree and no other buildings inside it. Why leave the middle of the circuit empty?

options.text: The court is the light and air the walk is built around, and keeping it open is what makes the covered route usable
The court is reserved for burials, so the open ground in the middle is the only part of the precinct available for the dead
options.misconception: supposes the court is a burial ground, when burials are outside the circuit

options.text: The court is a market space, since the sheltered sides of the square give traders a dry place to set up stalls
options.misconception: assigns a commercial function to a court enclosed within a religious precinct

options.text: The court is a defensive space, since an empty square gives watchmen a clear view of anyone approaching the walk
options.misconception: reads a monastic court as a defensive emplacement

questions.explanation: The emptiness is the point. A covered walk is only worth building if there is something to walk beside, and the open court is that something: it supplies daylight deep into the plan, air in a heated climate, and a view that changes with the hour and the season. Anyone standing at the arcade looks across the court to the opposite side, which doubles the apparent size of the enclosure and gives the walk a place to pause and to converse. A tree, a well or a covered structure can occupy the centre, but buildings do not, and the reason is structural as much as visual: a roofed mass in the middle would block the light the court exists to admit, and would have to be entered through the walk itself. The court is a garden in a building's plan, and its emptiness is the design.
questions.hint: Ask what a covered walk needs beside it, and what a roofed mass in the middle would do to the light.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The threat a fortified wall answers
questions.learningObjective: identify the assault a fortification is designed against
questions.stem: A town wall of thick masonry, high enough to be reached only by ladder, is described as topped with crenellations and machicolations. What is the wall built to answer?

options.text: Attackers at the foot of the wall, since the height denies a ladder and the projections allow the wall to be defended at its own base
Water rising in the town, since a thick masonry wall takes the flood pressure without any movement of the joints
options.misconception: treats a town wall as a flood barrier rather than a defence against people

options.text: Fire within the town, since a non-combustible wall keeps the blaze from jumping from roof to roof
options.misconception: reads a fortification as a fire break, which is a later urban idea

options.text: The weight of the buildings behind it, since a thick wall carries the roofs and the upper storeys that lean on it
options.misconception: treats a defensive wall as a load-bearing party wall for the town

questions.explanation: Every feature on the wall is a response to a person trying to get over it. Height matters because ladders are the only way up and a long ladder is hard to bring to a standstill under fire. Thickness matters because the base of a wall is where an attacker works, picking and burning at the masonry, and a thick wall can be defended at that level by dropping stones or boiling material through openings in the projecting parapet above. The crenellations are the same arrangement seen from the other side: the merlons cover the defenders and the embrasures let them shoot, so a wall is a firing step as much as a barrier. The wall behind a town is not a flood defence and not a fire break, and it is not carrying the roofs; it stands between the town and the people outside who would otherwise walk in.
questions.hint: Ask who is on the near side of the wall and who is on the far side, and what each side does there.

questions.topic: A described curtain wall read as a firing step
questions.learningObjective: read wall defences as positions for defenders
questions.stem: A section through a town wall is described: an earthen bank packed behind a thin outer face, with a stone parapet set at the top projecting beyond it. What does the section show about the wall's purpose?

options.text: The earth does the work of absorbing impact and the thin stone face resists the weather, while the projecting parapet gives defenders a covered platform
The stone is redundant, since a packed earth bank alone resists a battering ram as well as any masonry face
options.misconception: supposes packed earth alone resists impact, ignoring the facing that takes the blow

options.text: The parapet is decorative, since the height of the wall alone determines how well the wall can be defended
options.misconception: makes height the whole of the defence and ignores cover for the defenders

options.text: The wall is a retaining wall for the town behind it, since the bank is holding up the ground on which the houses stand
options.misconception: mistakes a defensive section for a retaining structure

questions.explanation: A section tells you where the material is doing the resisting, and here the material is shared. Packed earth is superb at absorbing a blow: it gives, it absorbs, and it does not crack, so the mass of the bank is what actually refuses a ram or a mine. A thin stone or timber face over it is then doing the other job, keeping rain and weather out of the bank and giving the masons a surface to build against. The parapet is a third thing again. By projecting beyond the wall face it creates a walkway with openings through the floor, so a defender can drop material on attackers working at the base while standing under cover. Height alone does not give cover, and the section shows a wall designed to be occupied as well as to be climbed.
questions.hint: Ask which part takes the impact, which part keeps the weather out, and what a projecting parapet lets a defender do.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a water-filled moat requires
questions.learningObjective: infer the water supply a moat implies
questions.stem: A castle ditch is described as holding standing water rather than being dry or planted. What does that choice commit the builders to?

options.text: A supply and a storage: water has to be brought in and held, and it will stagnate and have to be cleared and let in again
Nothing at all, since water in a ditch is the cheapest defence available and needs no maintenance of any kind
options.misconception: believes a wet ditch is maintenance free, when it is the opposite

options.text: A deep well inside the castle, since standing water is only possible where the ground itself is permanently saturated
options.misconception: assumes standing water means the ground is wet, ignoring an engineered supply

options.text: A second wall inside the ditch, since water alone cannot hold a wall up and a revetment must always back it
options.misconception: supposes a water-filled ditch always needs a revetted lining

questions.explanation: A dry ditch is a slope an attacker must climb; a ditch full of water is a gap they cannot cross, and the strength of the second depends on it being water. That single sentence introduces a permanent obligation. Water has to be available all year, which means a well, a stream diverted, a reservoir or a tank, and it has to be held, which means a lined ditch with a controlled level and an inlet. It also has to be kept moving, because a still ditch becomes a health problem and a breeding place; silt and rubbish must be cleared, and a dirty or foul ditch stops being a barrier and becomes a nuisance the garrison would rather have drained. A dry ditch is cheaper and simpler. A wet one is stronger, and it is stronger precisely because it is expensive to keep.
questions.hint: Ask what has to happen every year for water to still be in the ditch when an army arrives.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The second work a moat denies
questions.learningObjective: explain how a moat blocks tunnelling as well as approach
questions.stem: A castle's ditch is described as cut into soft ground and kept full of water. What second kind of attack does this combination prevent, besides a direct rush at the wall?

options.text: Mining, because a dig has to pass through wet ground and water flowing into the tunnel would flood the workings
Scaling, because a wet ditch gives an attacker nothing firm to set a scaling ladder against
options.misconception: confuses the footing under the ladder with the footing under the miner

options.text: Firing, because standing water in a ditch stops the besiegers from bringing forward their heavy guns
options.misconception: claims a ditch prevents artillery being brought up, which is a problem of roads

options.text: Escalade, because the wall cannot be climbed from inside a ditch that is full of water
options.misconception: confuses the defenders' ditch with the attacker's approach

questions.explanation: The classic way to take a wall is not to climb it but to go under it. A tunnelling party works from inside the ditch, braces a shaft, drives a passage towards the foundation, props it with timber, and sets the foundation on fire; the wall drops into the void. A ditch defeats that, and a wet one defeats it twice over. The soft ground under water is unstable, so a shaft cannot be safely sunk and the timbers cannot be braced; and once the workings are open, the ditch pours into them and the miners drown in their own gallery. That is why the ditch and the wall are usually built together as one work and why the spacing of the ditch from the wall matters as much as its depth. A water-filled ditch also disrupts the footing for ladders, but that is a secondary and much cheaper effect to obtain.
questions.hint: Ask what a besieging army does that starts in the ditch, and what happens when the ditch is full of water.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The height advantage of a keep
questions.learningObjective: explain the tactical advantage of a tall keep within a walled site
questions.stem: A keep stands inside the town walls, taller than every other building on the site, with a single entrance reached by a long stair. What does that height buy the garrison?

options.text: Sight over the walls and the ground beyond, so the defenders can see an approach while the attackers stay below the wall top
A commanding position for the garrison, so that in a dispute inside the town the side holding the keep can impose terms
options.misconception: leads with the internal contest, which the keep's height serves only incidentally

options.text: A place above the water in a flooded ditch, since the lower buildings of a castle could be submerged for months
options.misconception: supplies a flood refuge, which a keep does not specifically provide

options.text: A store of height for grain and timber, since a tall chamber is the only way to keep provisions dry above a damp ground floor
options.misconception: treats storey height as a storage problem rather than a defensive one

questions.explanation: A keep is the last place to be reached, and the whole of its design points outward. Its height gives the defenders a view over the curtain wall and the land beyond it, so an army can be watched while it is still assembling and its equipment identified from a distance. That view is worth more than the extra storeys it holds, and the fact that it is seen from above rather than from the side is the whole advantage. The single entrance up a long stair is the same logic reversed: a stair is slow to climb and impossible to hurry, and a wall is easier to break than a defended sequence of steps. The keep also settles internal disputes and gives a safe store, but those are secondary uses of a form whose primary argument is vertical, and the flood and grain explanations have nothing to do with why the tower is tall.
questions.hint: Ask what a defender standing at the top of the keep can do that a defender on the wall cannot.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A castle that becomes a residence
questions.learningObjective: explain why defensive forms survive after their function
questions.stem: A sixteenth-century residence is built with round towers, machicolated cornices and a dry moat, in a province where no army came for two hundred years. Why keep the military vocabulary?

options.text: The forms had become the sign of lordly authority, so the vocabulary was kept while the rooms behind it were made for living
The masonry was cheaper in those shapes, so the builders used towers because they were economical to erect
options.misconception: claims a structural economy that the choice of form does not rest on

options.text: The towers were still needed for defence, since small raiding bands continued to attack isolated houses
options.misconception: presumes a continuing military need where the account records no assault

options.text: The moat and towers were built for display alone, and the owner had no interest in how the house was defended
options.misconception: overstates the claim, since the forms were a claim rather than pure decoration

questions.explanation: By the sixteenth century a siege was decided by artillery, income and a state's army rather than by a tower, and a noble house in a quiet province was never going to be defended by machicolations. Yet the towers, the moat and the crowning parapet persist, and they persist because they had stopped being a description of a military function and become a description of a rank. Keeping a form whose defence has lapsed is a way of claiming a continuity: the house says that its owner stands where his family stood, and the vocabulary is inherited along with the land. The rooms behind the towers are comfortable, glazed and symmetrical, and they are arranged for court life rather than for a garrison. To read the towers as cheap to build is to mistake the appearance for the reason, and to read them as pure decoration is to understate the political work they do.
questions.hint: Ask what the towers would have been called by a visitor in the sixteenth century, and what the visitor would have understood.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The angle of a bastion face
questions.learningObjective: explain how an angled wall face removes a blind spot
questions.stem: In the new style of fortification the projecting corners are cut back into angled faces rather than left square, and the walls between them are lower and thicker than before. What does the angle buy?

options.text: It lets the defenders of one face shoot along the foot of the next face, so the ground at the base of the wall is no longer hidden
It lets the defenders shoot round the corner onto attackers who have already reached the wall on the adjoining face
options.misconception: describes only the frontal fire, missing the grazing fire along the base

options.text: It reduces the number of men needed to hold the circuit, since an angled face is shorter than the wall it replaces
options.misconception: reduces the problem to manning, when the angle is about fields of fire

options.text: It presents a stronger face to a battering ram, since a sloping wall turns a horizontal blow into a downward one
options.misconception: applies a raking argument to a weapon that cannot strike from above

questions.explanation: The blind spot of the old wall is geometric and it is obvious once you picture it. A square corner with two straight walls leaves a wedge of ground at the foot of the corner, out of sight of anyone on either wall, and it is exactly there that an attacking party collects with picks, ladders and bundles, undisturbed. Cutting the corner back into two angled faces removes the wedge and replaces it with two surfaces that can be seen from each other: a musket or a cannon on one face bears directly along the base of the other, and nothing at the foot of the work is now unobserved. The other two changes in the profile belong to the same century. A wall hit by a cannon must be thick enough not to shatter, and a thick wall cannot also be tall, so the works came down and grew outward. It is fire coverage and material, not economy, that the angle solves.
questions.hint: Draw the square corner and look at what is on the ground at its foot that neither wall can see.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A trace of a bastioned fort read as evidence
questions.learningObjective: interpret a described fort trace through its geometry and profile
questions.stem: A survey of a fort records: faces meeting at slightly obtuse angles, a rampart twelve metres high and six metres thick at the base, earthen banks behind the masonry, and covered positions arranged to command the ground between the faces. What does the record show?

options.text: A design answering artillery, since the profile is massive rather than tall and the angles exist to give the masonry a field of fire along its own base
A design answering ladders, since the twelve-metre height is the governing measurement and the angles are the builders' decoration
options.misconception: treats height as the governing measurement in a design made for guns

options.text: A siege work made by the besiegers, since a bank behind a rampart is what a besieging army throws up to gain height
options.misconception: assigns the work to the attackers, when the covered positions and angles defend the enclosure

options.text: A dry landscape, since the record shows no water anywhere and the bank is described as earth rather than masonry throughout
options.misconception: infers a dry site from earthen banks, which are ordinary in dry and wet alike

questions.explanation: Read the numbers and the profile answers to its own question. Twelve metres of height against six metres of thickness is a mass, not a screen, and a mass is what a wall needs when the blow comes from a cannon rather than from a battering ram: the wall has to be thick enough that the shot cannot shatter it through. The slightly obtuse angles are the second half of the same answer, since they exist so that the wall can be fired along by its own defenders and nothing collects unseen at the foot. The earthen banks behind the masonry are the earlier fortification still in the ground, absorbed rather than removed, which is common where a site was rebuilt in place. The covered positions command the ground between the faces, which is where an attack would come. Height was never the point in this profile; coverage was.
questions.hint: Compare the height with the thickness, and ask which weapon a wall has to be thick enough to survive.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The profile a tall wall assumes before artillery
questions.learningObjective: identify the weapon a tall thin wall profile presupposes
questions.stem: A medieval town wall is described as tall, thin, vertical and pierced by few openings, with a parapet high above the street. What does that profile assume about its attacker?

options.text: An attacker on foot at the base, who must bring his own ladders and cannot strike the wall from a distance
An attacker with siege guns, who will not bother to climb a wall he can open from three hundred paces
options.misconception: assumes the profile was designed against artillery, which is the opposite of the chronology

options.text: An attacker inside the town, since the wall is built to keep the inhabitants in rather than the enemy out
options.misconception: reverses the wall's direction of defence, which is from outside

options.text: An attacker with fire, since a high parapet catches the wind and keeps smoke from settling on the wall walk
options.misconception: gives a wall a smoke-control function it does not have

questions.explanation: A profile is an argument about the enemy, and this one says the enemy arrives on foot. Height denies a ladder, and a tall thin wall is the most efficient possible way to deny a ladder, because the material spent goes upward where the attacker's effort is concentrated rather than sideways where it is not. Few openings is the same decision again: an embrasure is a hole in the wall, and a wall built to be climbed is not a wall with holes in it. All of it assumes the enemy brings his own means of ascent and has no means of striking at a distance. That assumption held for a long time, and when it stopped holding the wall did not get taller; it came down, thickened and turned its face outward, because a cannonball does not have to be carried to the wall at all.
questions.hint: Ask what the enemy has to bring to the foot of the wall, and whether he has to bring it at all.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The three changes artillery forced in a wall
questions.learningObjective: connect wall profile changes to the effect of cannon fire
questions.stem: When guns could strike a wall from a distance, the accepted profile became low, thick and angled rather than high, thin and square. What does each change answer?

options.text: Thickness so the wall resists being shattered at a distance, low so it presents less target, and angled so it is not a flat face to be battered
Thickness so more masons are employed, low so the ditch can be dug deeper, and angled so rainwater runs off the face
options.misconception: supplies labour and drainage reasons for a profile set by ballistics

options.text: Thickness so the wall resists fire, low so the defenders can be seen from the town, and angled so the ditch can drain
options.misconception: attributes a fire-resistant function to a wall defence profile

options.text: Thickness so the wall carries a raised walkway, low so the material costs less, and angled so the corners shed snow
options.misconception: reads the profile as economy and weather, ignoring the impact it must survive

questions.explanation: Each of the three terms answers a separate consequence of the same change in weapons. A cannon delivers its energy at a distance and can be moved to another target, so a wall has to survive a blow rather than merely resist a batter, and surviving a blow means depth: enough stone that the shot buries itself in the face. The same accuracy removes the value of height, because a tall wall is simply more wall to be hit and no longer denies a ladder to a man who can shoot at the parapet from a hundred paces. The angle is the third consequence, and it is the least obvious: a flat masonry face takes the impact square and offers a face to be undermined, whereas a sloping face turns much of the impact into a load carried down into the earth behind it. The works got lower, thicker and oblique, and the old walls stayed standing as ruins and as second walls behind the new.
questions.hint: Take each of the three words and ask which part of the impact it deals with.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Scour at the base of a bridge pier
questions.learningObjective: explain how flowing water removes the bed beneath a pier
questions.stem: At an old stone bridge, the river bed is described as much deeper immediately downstream of a pier than in mid-channel, and the hole has grown measurably over fifty years. What is happening there?

options.text: The pier is obstructing the flow, so the water speeds up around it and drops the sediment that was holding the bed up
The pier is settling under load, so the masonry has sunk and left a step in the bed that water has not yet filled
options.misconception: reads a scour hole as settlement, though settlement is uniform rather than a hole

options.text: Barge traffic is dragging gravel from under the pier each time it passes, and the hole is the record of the towpath
options.misconception: attributes the hole to a single recurring cause in a channel governed by flow

options.text: The river is deepening as a whole because of upstream quarrying, and the pier is only marking where the water is already deepest
options.misconception: explains a local hole by a general cause, when the cause is local obstruction

questions.explanation: Scour is a flow problem before it is a structural one. A pier standing in a current divides it: the water is forced to accelerate as it squeezes past, and on the downstream side a swirling eddy forms in which the speed is high enough to lift sand and gravel out of the bed. Whatever the pier is founded on is then carried away, and the hole deepens because a deeper hole lets the water move faster still, which carries away more. That is why scour is progressive and why it is measured over years rather than noticed in a flood. The same mechanism works with sediment, but the accelerator is the pier itself, and it explains why the hole is immediately behind the pier and not spread evenly along the channel. A settling pier leans and cracks; it does not dig a hole, and a uniform deepening would not gather at one obstacle.
questions.hint: Ask what the water has to do when a pier is in its way, and where the fastest water is.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A cutwater described on a pier
questions.learningObjective: read a cutwater as a device for controlling flow at a pier
questions.stem: A bridge pier is described as ending upstream in a semicircular projection and downstream in a point, with the masonry footing measurably wider than the shaft above it. What is each of those features for?

options.text: The upstream round end splits the current so it slides around the pier, and the wide footing resists the sideways force the flow still exerts
Both ends are carved to carry a commemorative panel, and the wider footing holds the extra masonry those panels required
options.misconception: reads a hydraulic device as commemorative carving and its base as display

options.text: The upstream projection is there to turn floating debris away from the deck, and the point downstream lets the pier be rebuilt in sections
options.misconception: assigns the projection to debris and the point to a construction sequence

options.text: The round upstream end reduces the amount of stone needed, and the point downstream carries the roadway over the pier more neatly
options.misconception: supplies an economy and an appearance reason for a shape set by water

questions.explanation: Water meeting a flat face does two damaging things: it stops dead and builds pressure against the face, and it separates from the surface with a curl that dives down along the wall and digs at the masonry just past the edge. A cutwater answers the first, because a rounded or pointed end presents no flat face for the current to press on, and water that meets a curve is turned aside and passed along rather than held. The shape is set to suit the flow: round where the current arrives head-on, pointed where the divided streams rejoin behind the pier, since a point is what keeps the rejoining turbulence from working at the masonry. The wide footing is the second, separate measure. Even with a good end, a pier takes a sideways push in flood, and a footing that spreads into the bed resists being tipped, which is why the base is the widest part of the whole bridge.
questions.hint: Ask what water does when it hits a flat face, and what it does with the sand and gravel it is carrying.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What carries a suspended deck
questions.learningObjective: trace the forces in a cable-stayed or suspended deck
questions.stem: A bridge deck is described as slung from vertical hangers hung on two great cables, which pass over the tops of two towers and run down to blocks of masonry at each end. What is actually holding the deck up?

options.text: The cables, which are in tension: each carries the weight of the deck down the slope of the cable and out into the anchorages
The towers, which take the whole weight down to their foundations while the cables only keep the deck from swinging
options.misconception: loads the towers with the deck, ignoring that the cables carry it to the anchorages

options.text: The hangers, which act as short struts in compression and transfer the deck load to the deck itself
options.misconception: calls the hangers compression members when they are ties in tension

options.text: The anchorages, whose weight alone resists the pull of the cables without any need of the towers
options.misconception: supplies a suspension bridge with no towers, which the described arrangement requires

questions.explanation: Follow the forces along the described path and they are unambiguous. The deck hangs from hangers, the hangers pull down on the cable, and a cable can only pull. So the cable is in tension, and because a tension member is only as good as what holds its ends, the cable has to be carried over something that raises it and anchored to something that resists its pull. The towers raise the cable so that the span between them is a curve with a useful sag, and the anchorages at each end take the horizontal component of the pull and the vertical component into the ground. The tower bases do carry a large load, but they carry the cable's pull and not the deck's weight, which is the distinction the arrangement turns on. That is also why a suspension bridge can span further than any arch: the cable can be made longer, whereas an arch needs more height for the same span.
questions.hint: Ask what a cable can do, then ask what has to hold each of its two ends.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Cable and anchorage as two separate jobs
questions.learningObjective: separate the carrying function of a cable from the holding function of an anchorage
questions.stem: A suspension bridge is described with cables carried over towers and made fast at block-like masses of masonry at each end. First say what the cable does with the load of the deck, and then say what the anchorage does with the cable's pull.

options.text: The cable carries the deck in tension down its slope, and the anchorage resists the horizontal pull that tension creates
The cable compresses the deck along its length, and the anchorage holds the towers upright against the resulting weight
options.misconception: makes a cable a compression member and misassigns the anchorage's work

options.text: The cable only keeps the deck level, and the anchorage carries the deck load into the ground on each shore
options.misconception: reduces the cable to levelling and gives the anchorage the deck

options.text: The cable transfers the deck load to the tower tops, and the anchorage merely stops the cable from sliding down past the towers
options.misconception: puts the deck on the towers and reduces the anchorage to a stop

questions.explanation: Split the question and each half has its own answer. The cable's job is to carry: the hangers hang the deck from it, a cable resists being pulled straight, so the load travels along the cable and down through the towers into their foundations, with the cable itself in tension throughout. The anchorage's job is to hold: at each end the cable pulls in two directions at once, straight down towards the shore and horizontally inwards along the span, and the block of masonry is there to resist that pair, which is why it is a mass rather than a post and why it is often the largest single foundation on the site. Treating these as one job is the usual confusion, and it produces the belief that the towers carry the deck. They carry the cable, which is a different statement with a different consequence for the sizing of every part.
questions.hint: Ask which member pulls, and then ask which member is being dragged towards the middle of the span.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: How a masonry bridge carries a road
questions.learningObjective: trace the load of a road over a series of arches
questions.stem: A masonry bridge is described as a ring of wedge-shaped stones over each opening, with the space between the ring and the roadway packed with rubble. Where does the weight of the traffic go?

options.text: Through the rubble onto the ring, and around the ring into the abutments, so the roadway's weight becomes thrust at the banks
Straight down through the ring into the river bed, so the arch is only there to keep the water out of the fill
options.misconception: sends the load straight down through the ring, when it travels round the curve

options.text: Into the spandrel walls, which act as retaining walls for the fill and pass it to the piers beneath the roadway
options.misconception: makes the spandrel the carrier, when it retains fill and passes thrust to the arch

options.text: Into the ring's keystone, which takes the whole weight and passes it down through the centre of the opening
options.misconception: loads the keystone, which is the closing stone and not the collector of the weight

questions.explanation: The rubble is not structural fill; it is the load. A road is a continuous heavy surface sitting above a row of openings, and that weight has to reach the ground, but it cannot reach the ground through the water. So the weight passes into the arch itself at the crown, travels round the curve in compression, and leaves at the springings as a sideways push which the abutments and the piers between the openings take back into the ground. The spandrel walls are the faces that retain the fill and keep the roadway from spilling out, and their job is containment rather than carriage, though they add weight exactly where the arch is already working hardest. This is why an old masonry bridge is vulnerable at its piers: the whole weight of the road behind a pier is pushing at it from one side and nothing at all from the other, which is a problem for the foundation rather than the arch.
questions.hint: Ask where the weight of the road can actually go, given that the middle of the opening is water.

questions.topic: Why a cantilever needs a counterweight
questions.learningObjective: explain the balance a cantilever depends on
questions.stem: A projecting stone gallery is described as reaching out from a wall with a heavy mass of masonry stacked above its inboard end. What is holding the projecting end up?

options.text: The weight stacked behind it, which presses down on the inboard arm and offsets the moment of the projecting arm about the support
The strength of the stone in the projecting arm, which is a beam resting on the wall and needs no mass behind it at all
options.misconception: treats a cantilever as a simple beam, which is the mistake the counterweight answers

options.text: The bond of the wall behind it, since the gallery is simply the wall turned sideways and inherits the wall's own stability
options.misconception: supposes the gallery inherits the wall's stability without a balancing mass

options.text: The friction of the joint where the gallery meets the wall, since the stone is rough enough to prevent the arm sliding
options.misconception: rests the cantilever on friction at a joint, which is not what carries it

questions.explanation: A cantilever is an unbalanced arm, and unbalanced means it turns. The projecting gallery wants to rotate downwards about the point where it leaves the wall, and the only thing that stops a mass of stone rotating is a mass of stone on the other side of the pivot. So the builders put a parapet or a storey above the inboard end, and the weight of it holds the far end up. That is the whole trick, and it explains the form: the heavy part of a cantilever is always the part nobody sees, and the part that projects is the light one. It is also why a cantilever in brittle stone is built in a few courses with the heaviest at the back, and why the support has to be wide enough to take the moment without being crushed or turned. Treating it as a beam resting on a wall is the natural error, and it is what the counterweight exists to correct.
questions.hint: Ask which way an unbalanced arm wants to turn, and what would counter that turn.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The fire risk of an unprotected metal frame
questions.learningObjective: explain why a metal frame had to be encased
questions.stem: An early tall building of iron and steel frame is described as clad in the same wood and plaster as the buildings around it, with nothing between the frame members and the outer wall. What risk followed from that detail?

options.text: Fire travelled through the frame, since a continuous metal structure conducts heat and does not char away like timber, so the whole storey could go at once
The frame rusted faster than a masonry wall, since iron in a damp cavity corrodes and a stone wall does not
options.misconception: leads with corrosion, which is a durability problem rather than the described one

options.text: The cladding fell off in a high wind, since thin sheets cannot be fixed to a metal frame that moves under temperature change
options.misconception: makes cladding detachment the risk, when the described material is the problem

options.text: The building was too stiff for its foundations, since a metal frame is far less rigid than a wall of the same height
options.misconception: claims a metal frame is too flexible, which is not why the encasing was needed

questions.explanation: The detail that matters is the absence of anything between the frame and the outside. Timber behaves in a fire by charring: the outside burns, the charred layer insulates, and the section of the member that survives is the part that is still unburnt, so a wooden frame can outlast its own surface fire. A metal frame does not char; it heats, conducts and loses strength, and a member that has lost strength is still a member still carrying the floors above it. The result is that heat travels along the structure and the fire spreads through the building rather than being held to one room. The remedy followed directly: enclose the frame in a material that does char, such as brick, tile or boarded and plastered construction, and the metal becomes the structure while the enclosure becomes the fire protection. Steel frames made height possible and then had to be hidden to keep the building standing.
questions.hint: Compare what a wooden beam does in a fire with what a steel beam does, and ask which one lets heat pass along it.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: An encased frame read after a fire
questions.learningObjective: read a described frame enclosure as fire protection
questions.stem: A building survives a fire with its floors in place, while the rooms above the fire are burnt through. The report notes that the iron columns inside the wall cavity are deformed but not melted, and that brick arches were found between them. What does the description show?

options.text: That the frame took the heat and deformed while the brick between it stayed cold enough to survive, which is what the enclosure is for
That the fire was small, since a serious fire would have melted iron columns rather than bending them
options.misconception: judges the fire's size from the fate of the metal, ignoring what an enclosure does

options.text: That the columns were the original timber, since iron cannot be deformed in a fire and can only melt
options.misconception: assumes iron has no intermediate state between sound and liquid

options.text: That the brick arches are a later repair, since a fireproof enclosure would have prevented the floors from burning at all
options.misconception: overstates what fireproofing promises, since it protects the frame rather than the contents

questions.explanation: Iron loses strength long before it melts, and a member that has lost strength sags and buckles while still in its solid state, so a deformed but unmelted column is exactly what a hot steel frame looks like. The informative part of the report is the pairing: the metal was in the cavity and the brick was between it and the rooms, and the two behaved differently for the same reason. Brick is poor at conducting heat and it does not lose strength at the temperatures a room fire reaches, so the arcading between the columns absorbed the passage of time and gave the fire something to stop at. That is the whole purpose of encasing a frame, and it is why a fire can gut a building and leave the skeleton standing. Nothing about the outcome suggests a small fire, and the floors were never going to be protected by a wall treatment.
questions.hint: Ask where the heat went, given that one material was inside the cavity and the other was between it and the rooms.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A tall building's wall as a hung skin
questions.learningObjective: state what changes when a wall no longer carries the building
questions.stem: The outer wall of a tall building is described as being hung on the frame, carried at each floor and supporting nothing above it. What does that change?

options.text: The wall becomes a screen rather than a structure, so the floors can be open inside and the openings can be as large as the frame allows
The wall becomes heavier, since it has to hang from the frame without the help of the masonry below it
options.misconception: claims a hung wall is heavier, when the load is small by design

options.text: The building becomes stiffer, since a frame clad on the outside resists wind better than a solid wall of the same height
options.misconception: attributes stiffness to the cladding rather than to the frame

options.text: The wall can be any material at all, since a non-structural screen is unaffected by the material of the frame behind it
options.misconception: claims total material freedom, ignoring the fixings that carry the screen

questions.explanation: The word that matters is carried. A load-bearing wall supports everything above it, which means its thickness has to increase as the building rises, which means its openings get smaller and the floors get darker and more fixed, because the wall is dictating the plan. A wall that is hung at each floor is a skin, and then the structure is the frame alone. The interior of the building becomes a set of floors and columns that the occupant arranges, and the window can be as large as the frame and the wind allow rather than as large as the bearing wall permits. This is a change in who decides the plan, from the wall to the frame. The skin itself is not weightless and its material is still constrained by how it is fixed and by how it weathers, but its job is to close the building and keep the weather out, which is a far smaller job than carrying it.
questions.hint: Ask what changes for the person inside when the wall is no longer the thing that holds the building up.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The material that made height possible
questions.learningObjective: explain why a metal skeleton changed the possible height of a building
questions.stem: A building is described as a skeleton of slender metal columns and beams with the floors and the walls hung on it, rising far higher than anything built in timber or in load-bearing masonry. What in the material made that possible?

options.text: It takes tension as well as compression, so a member can be thin and joined, where stone and timber must be sized by the load they carry in bending
It is fireproof, so the frame can carry the building without any enclosure between the metal and the outside air
options.misconception: claims a metal frame needs no fire protection, which is the opposite of the record

options.text: It is cheaper than stone, so the same money buys a taller structure than a masonry wall of the same base
options.misconception: makes cost the enabling property, when it is the range of forces the material can take

options.text: It can be cast in one piece, so a whole column arrives on site and needs no joints or connections to the floor above
options.misconception: supplies a single-piece column, whereas the frame depends on connections

questions.explanation: Height is limited by what a material can do in tension. Stone and timber are excellent in compression and poor in tension, so a member of either has to be deep enough to span by bending alone, and depth means weight, and weight at the bottom of a tall building is what makes the foundations the real problem. A metal frame changes the calculation because the connections can be made to take tension: wind on one face pulls and wind on the other pushes, and a frame that resists both behaves as a single whole rather than as a stack of members each trying to stand up alone. That is why the skeleton can be slender and why the height then becomes a matter of foundations and wind rather than of the weight of the wall. Fire is a real problem for the same material and it had to be answered separately, but cost and castability are consequences rather than the reason the frame works.
questions.hint: Ask which force a stone member cannot take, and what a frame has to resist when the wind reverses.
