questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a civic building claims by its scale
questions.learningObjective: explain monumentality as a claim rather than a style
questions.stem: A civic building stands on a raised platform at the head of a broad square, with a facade articulated in columns and a roofline above every house around it. What is the building doing?

options.text: Claiming to represent a whole community, since its height, its isolated position and its formal frontage put it above the private buildings it governs
Admitting that the town could not afford more, since a building of that size took every resource the community had for years
options.misconception: reads the cost of the building as an account of its meaning

options.text: Keeping the square open, since a low building on an open site defends the ground better than a tall one would
options.misconception: supplies a defensive reason for a civic composition

options.text: Following the classical orders, since the columns are borrowed from a temple and the reference therefore settles the building's meaning
options.misconception: treats the vocabulary as the message, ignoring the position and scale

questions.explanation: Monumentality is a claim made in three materials at once. The height puts the building above the domestic scale of the town, which says that whatever it holds is not one household's business. The platform and the open square set it apart, so it is approached rather than entered from the street, and the approach is part of the argument. The formal frontage, with its symmetry and its classical orders borrowed from the language of temples and courts, presents the institution as permanent and orderly rather than as a temporary committee. None of this is decoration. The cost of the building is a fact about how it was paid for and has no bearing on what it claims, an open square does not defend ground, and the classical vocabulary is the least of the three because it is the part that is easiest to copy. Remove the position and the scale and the reference is only a style.
questions.hint: Ask what a viewer can tell about the importance of a building from where it stands and how high it is.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A survey of a planned capital
questions.learningObjective: interpret a described plan as one imposed geometric scheme
questions.stem: A survey of a planned capital records streets in a rectangular lattice of roughly one hundred metres by one hundred, a broad avenue cutting the grid and running for more than a kilometre, and a large open place set where two axes cross. What does the survey establish?

options.text: A single imposed scheme, since the lattice, the long avenue and the crossing place all belong to one geometry set out before the blocks were built
A later overlay, since a lattice over a long avenue and a square can only have been added after the town already existed
options.misconception: insists the layers must be successive when one geometry explains all three

options.text: An old road reused, since an avenue that runs for a kilometre must follow a route that was there first
options.misconception: assumes a long straight line can only come from a pre-existing route

options.text: A market, since a large open place at a crossing is always the site of an earlier market that the town grew around
options.misconception: reduces the whole survey to one feature's presumed earlier use

questions.explanation: The value of a survey is that it lets three features be tested against one another, and here they agree. A lattice at roughly regular intervals, a straight avenue running for more than a kilometre across it, and a place of the right size at the intersection of two axes are not three accidents of growth. A straight line a kilometre long can only be set out deliberately, the lattice can only be laid out deliberately, and the two are the same act of measurement because the avenue is straight through a grid that is regular in both directions. The crossing place is the logical consequence, since an axis needs a terminus and a square is what a terminus looks like. Read together, the record is a drawing office: the geometry came first and the blocks were filled in afterwards, which is the ordinary sequence in a planned capital and the reason the plan is legible from the air.
questions.hint: Ask whether three features can be explained by one measurement or need three separate accidents.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a continuous street frontage does
questions.learningObjective: explain how a common frontage turns a street into a space
questions.stem: Along a broad avenue the facades of the buildings are set back to the same line and rise to roughly the same height. What has the street done to the buildings?

options.text: Turned a row of separate plots into one continuous enclosure, so the street reads as an outdoor room rather than as a gap between buildings
Made every building identical, since a shared frontage and height leave no room for differences between the owners who built them
options.misconception: infers uniformity of building from uniformity of the street line

options.text: Widened the pavement, since the buildings have been pulled back far enough to give the footway the space the traffic needs
options.misconception: reads a set-back frontage as a widened pavement for traffic

options.text: Raised the rents, since a common height limits the number of storeys each owner may build and so restricts the floor area on offer
options.misconception: takes an economic effect to be the design intention of the street

questions.explanation: A street is not the space between buildings; it is a space that buildings make. What the eye needs to read a street as a room is a continuous edge and a consistent height, because those two together give the space a floor and a ceiling and let the whole length be seen as one thing. Set every facade on one line and every cornice at one level, and the avenue acquires a wall, and the effect is additive rather than subtractive: nothing forces the buildings to be alike inside or behind, and the differences the owners want are all still there. The pavement, the trees and the width of the carriageway are other matters, and the rent effect, though real, is a consequence rather than the reason for a rule about cornice lines. The point of the rule is that the street will be read as a single designed space rather than as a run of unrelated buildings.
questions.hint: Ask what the eye needs at the edges of an outdoor space in order to read it as one space.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a frontage rule produces
questions.learningObjective: predict the urban effect of a continuous frontage and arcades
questions.stem: The regulations for a new avenue specify a uniform building height, an unbroken frontage line, and arcades at pavement level along the whole length. What follows from all three together?

options.text: A continuous street wall with a sheltered edge, so the avenue works as a place to walk and to stop as well as a route for traffic
A cheaper street, since uniform height and a shared facade line let the builders reuse one set of drawings for every plot
options.misconception: attributes an economic gain that is not what the three rules are for

options.text: A wider carriageway, since the arcades are set back far enough from the frontage to allow two more lanes of traffic
options.misconception: claims the arcades gain carriageway rather than shelter the footway

options.text: A closed street, since an unbroken frontage on both sides prevents light and air from reaching the middle of the avenue
options.misconception: treats continuity as a barrier to light rather than as an enclosure

questions.explanation: Take the three rules as one design rather than three regulations. The uniform height gives the avenue a ceiling line; the unbroken frontage gives it a wall; and the arcades at pavement level give the wall a use. A continuous wall with a roofed walk at its foot is the difference between a street that is only a route and a street that is a place, because the arcade shelters pedestrians from the traffic and from the weather and offers somewhere to stand, shop and wait at the edge of the moving stream. This is a nineteenth-century solution to a nineteenth-century problem, which is that widening a street for traffic strips it of everything that made it worth widening. The rules do not cheapen the work, since repeating a drawing is not the point and the plots are not identical, and continuity is enclosure rather than confinement: the space between two walls is more legible, not less.
questions.hint: Combine the three rules and ask what a person on the footway can now do that the traffic would have prevented.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A park described as enclosed ground
questions.learningObjective: infer what a designed park displaced
questions.stem: A public park is described as laid out with a continuous circuit walk, clumps of trees, open lawns and a lake, with gates at each of four points and houses built up right up to the boundary. What has been done to the ground?

options.text: Former common grazing and scattered use has been given a designed shape, a circuit and an edge, and the walks now keep people to a chosen route
A landscape of older gardens has simply been opened to the public, since a circuit walk cannot be laid out from nothing
options.misconception: assumes a designed park must be an old garden opened up rather than new ground

options.text: Nothing has changed, since ground used for grazing and ground laid out as a park are both open and the difference is only in the planting
options.misconception: denies that a circuit, a boundary and a lake change how ground is used

options.text: A market has been enclosed, since the gates at four points and the boundary wall are the remains of a trading enclosure
options.misconception: reads gates and a boundary as remains of a market rather than as park design

questions.explanation: A park is an argument about how land is used, and the description contains the argument. Before the circuit there was open ground used opportunistically: grazing, gathering, short-cut routes, whatever the season allowed, with no defined edge and no reason to stay on any particular line. The circuit walk is the decisive addition, because it is a rule about where people go, and everything else in the design supports it: the lake, the lawns and the tree clumps are placed as destinations and screens along a route that can be walked without a map. Four gates and a hard boundary then close the park against the street, which is the opposite of the earlier open ground. The result is land made legible and programmed, and the houses at the boundary are the price of that legibility, since a park with a frontage of small buildings is a room in a city rather than a piece of countryside.
questions.hint: Ask what the circuit walk does to where people walk, and what the boundary does to who can use the ground.

questions.topic: A tower described as out of plumb
questions.learningObjective: infer the ground condition behind a leaning tower
questions.stem: A masonry bell tower is described as standing several metres out of plumb by the time it was finished, continuing to move slowly afterwards, and founded on a bed of soft compressible ground saturated with water. What does the description show?

options.text: That the foundation settled unevenly because the ground beneath it compacted, and the tower rotated as the far side sank
That the tower was built out of plumb on purpose, since a slight lean was a known device for giving a tower character
options.misconception: reads a documented settlement as an intentional device of the builder

options.text: That the belfry above is heavier than the base below, so the whole shaft has been pulled over by the weight of the bells
options.misconception: supposes a top-heavy shaft is the cause of a lean that began at the foundation

options.text: That the tower is a copy of an older leaning tower and was never intended to stand square
options.misconception: invents a copy relationship for a movement explained by the ground

questions.explanation: The description gives the cause in the same sentence as the effect, and the effect is continuous movement. A saturated, compressible bed has no fixed volume: when the weight of the masonry is put on it the water is squeezed out of the soil and the soil settles, and it settles more on the side where the soil is softer or more heavily loaded. A tall shaft on a foundation that has turned in plan does not stay vertical; it leans as it rotates, and it keeps leaning as long as the settlement goes on, which is why the movement is described as slow and continuing. That is a ground problem, and it is why towers of this kind have been extended, underpinned or monitored rather than straightened. A deliberate lean would be a decision about appearance, not a result that grows over years, and the weight of a belfry is a fraction of the whole shaft and acts far above the base.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to a foundation bed when a heavy load is put on it, and why the movement would not stop at one moment.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A dry ditch as an obstacle
questions.learningObjective: explain what a dry ditch still achieves
questions.stem: The ditch outside a castle wall is described as dry, planted with grass and scrub, and crossed by a single ramp. What is the ditch still doing?

options.text: It keeps attackers off the foot of the wall, so no one can reach the base to pick at it, ram it or mine under it
Nothing, since a ditch without water is only a hollow in the ground and offers no obstacle worth naming
options.misconception: dismisses a dry ditch, when the drop and the delay are the obstacle

options.text: It is a garden, since grass and scrub growing in it show the garrison had no use for the ground
options.misconception: reads planting as abandonment rather than as later use of a defence work

options.text: It is a ford, since the ramp through it is the point where a river crossing was carried out under the wall
options.misconception: assumes a crossing, where the ramp is the controlled access to the gate

questions.explanation: The valuable part of a ditch is not the water in it. A water-filled ditch is better because a wet ditch also stops tunnelling, but a dry ditch still forces an approaching party to cross a drop in full view, from a fixed point, slowly and in formation, with the wall above able to shoot at them while they are strung out and unable to use their numbers. The second job is subtler and older: the ditch is a clear zone. Nobody can stand at the foot of a wall in a ditch, which is exactly where picks and rams and a mine heading have to work, so the ditch denies the three attacks that operate at ground level while making the fourth, the ladder assault, more dangerous rather than less. Grass and scrub are later occupation of a work that has outlived its use, and the ramp is the one place where the delay has to be given up.
questions.hint: Ask what a wall cannot be defended against at its own foot, and what the ditch is doing to the ground there.

questions.topic: Relocation figures from a clearance scheme
questions.learningObjective: interpret clearance statistics as displacement
questions.stem: A municipal record reports that a district was declared unfit, that 2,400 dwellings in it were demolished over four years, and that the households displaced were rehoused in new estates on the edge of the town. What does the record show?

options.text: That the health problem was solved by moving people out, at the cost of their existing neighbourhoods, networks and access to work
That the district was rebuilt in place with better housing, since the demolished dwellings were replaced on the same site
options.misconception: relocates the rehousing, which the record places outside the district

options.text: That the clearance was a failure of the housing supply, since four years of demolition produced no new houses at all
options.misconception: denies the rehousing the record describes in the outer estates

options.text: That the population was unchanged, since rehousing people elsewhere necessarily keeps the town's numbers the same
options.misconception: assumes rehousing must be a closed movement, when the record speaks of estates at the edge

questions.explanation: Read the record as a sequence and the sequence is the argument. A district is declared unfit, the dwellings come down, and the households go to new estates at the edge of the town. The housing that replaces the slums is real and often better by the measures of the day: water, drainage, light, and space between buildings. What the record also shows is that the condition was treated as a property of the buildings rather than of the district, and the remedy followed the property. Distance is the cost, and it is a cost that does not appear in any line of the record: the new estates had cheap land, but the households lost the proximity to their work, to their kin and to the support networks that were the practical reason the old district had survived at all. A scheme of this kind is therefore a public health measure and a relocation at the same time, and reading it as only one of the two misstates it.
questions.hint: Ask what kind of thing the scheme treated as the problem, and where the record says the people went.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Ridership and permits along a new transit line
questions.learningObjective: read transit data as induced development
questions.stem: A report on a new tram line records that passenger journeys tripled in its first two years, that building permits along the first three kilometres rose more than fourfold, and that the increase was strongest at the four terminus sites. What does the report show?

options.text: That the line made land buildable, because a reliable journey to work turned distant ground into somewhere worth a house
That the line was built along an already built-up corridor, since permits never rise before a street is laid
options.misconception: reverses cause and effect, when the permits follow the line

options.text: That the termini are the only parts of the line that matter, since the middle of the corridor is already fully developed
options.misconception: reduces a corridor effect to the ends, when the report shows a gradient

options.text: That the increase in journeys is a sign of falling rents, since more people travelling means less demand for housing near the centre
options.misconception: infers falling rents, which is the opposite of what permits rising implies

questions.explanation: The three figures have to be read together and in the right order. A tram line is a piece of infrastructure that changes the relationship between where people live and where they work, and the effect is strongest where the change is largest. That is the termini, where the journey time to the centre changes most, and the permits there rose fastest, which is the signature of induced development rather than of an independent building boom. In between, the corridor had better access too, but it also already had houses, so the pressure appears as additions, subdivisions and higher prices rather than as new construction on open ground. The tripled ridership is the mechanism, not the conclusion: more journeys mean more people living within reach of the line, and more people within reach means builders put up houses. This is why tram and railway lines are argued over as planning instruments, since the line is also a permission to develop.
questions.hint: Ask what the line changes about the journey to work, and where that change would be worth the most.

questions.topic: A column grid described in a survey
questions.learningObjective: interpret a recorded column grid as a span limit
questions.stem: A survey of a hall records 134 stone columns set in straight rows, spaced at a uniform 3.4 metres centre to centre in both directions, with a single architrave course running above them and no arches or vaults anywhere in the roof. What does the record show?

options.text: A roof spanning from column to column, so the width of every bay is set by how far a horizontal stone member can reach
A roof carried by walls, since the columns are decorative and the real support is in the outer walls
options.misconception: makes the columns decorative when they carry the whole roof

options.text: A frame of two storeys, since the uniform spacing of the columns indicates an upper level of galleries
options.misconception: reads a horizontal spacing as evidence of a second storey

options.text: An unfinished hall, since a roof with no arch or vault can only be a temporary covering put on before the vaulting was begun
options.misconception: calls a post-and-lintel roof temporary when it is a finished system

questions.explanation: The count and the spacing are the evidence, and they work together. A uniform 3.4 metres in both directions means the grid was set out by measurement, which is what a hall of this size requires so that the roof can be laid level and the architraves run straight. The absence of any arch or vault is the second fact, and it is a positive statement: the roof is carried directly on the architraves, and those are horizontal stone members, so each one can only reach from one column to the next. The bay spacing is therefore not a stylistic preference at all; it is the span limit of the material being used, which is why the number is so regular and why the number of columns is so large. A post-and-lintel roof is a finished system, not a temporary one, and the columns in it carry the entire roof rather than decorating a wall.
questions.hint: Ask what the roof is resting on, and what limits the distance between one column and the next.

questions.topic: Soundings around a bridge pier
questions.learningObjective: distinguish local scour from a general change of bed level
questions.stem: Soundings across a channel record the bed at 2 metres on the upstream side of a pier, 6 metres immediately downstream of it, and 2 metres again in mid-channel 200 metres away. What does the record show?

options.text: A local hole caused by the pier, since the bed is unchanged upstream and at mid-channel and only disturbed in the pier's own shadow
A general deepening of the channel, since every reading is at least two metres below the level of the banks
options.misconception: calls a single deep reading general, when the rest of the channel is normal

options.text: A settling foundation, since the hole is where the pier is and the pier has dropped by four metres
options.misconception: confuses a hole in the bed with a drop in the structure

options.text: A deposit that has built up over the pier, since material carried by the river has raised the bed there over the years
options.misconception: reads the deepest reading as the highest one, which is deposition

questions.explanation: The three readings make an argument on their own, because there is a control in them. The bed is at 2 metres upstream of the pier and 2 metres again in mid-channel, so 2 metres is the normal level of the bed here, and 6 metres is a hole. A hole at one place and a normal bed everywhere else cannot be a general deepening of the channel, and it cannot be deposition either, since deposition raises the bed rather than cutting it down. That leaves the pier, and the mechanism is the one the geometry dictates: the flow is obstructed, accelerates as it squeezes past, and drops the sediment behind the pier into a swirling bed that is scoured deeper with every season. The practical consequence is that the pier is founded in the hole, and a foundation that has lost its bearing needs either a cutwater, a wider base or protection of the bed around it.
questions.hint: Ask what the normal bed level is here, and what the difference between the readings measures.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: From defensive work to residence
questions.learningObjective: separate the moment a castle stops being a fortress from the moment it becomes a house
questions.stem: A great house of the sixteenth century keeps towers, a moat and thick walls, and its rooms are glazed, symmetrical and arranged for court life. First say what made the defensive parts useless, and then say what kept their forms in use.

options.text: Artillery and standing armies made the walls untakeable by any local lord, and the forms stayed because they had come to mean noble authority
Gunpowder made the walls flammable, and the forms stayed because the masons of the region could build nothing else
options.misconception: misstates what artillery did, and credits a building habit with keeping the forms

options.text: The moat was drained, so the walls lost their purpose, and the forms stayed because the owner could not afford to alter them
options.misconception: makes a drained moat the cause and poverty the reason the forms survived

options.text: The crown ordered the walls demolished, so the towers remain only as a record of what the survey found
options.misconception: invents an official demolition that the description does not record

questions.explanation: Split the question and the two halves explain each other. The defensive apparatus stops working when the decision about taking a castle is taken by an army with guns and a state's revenue behind it, because no household can hold out against a siege conducted for months by professionals, and the tall wall and its ditch are exactly the profile that guns defeat. What replaced it was not privacy but standing: the tower, the moat and the machicolated cornice had by then been read for centuries as the sign of lordship, so an owner building a house in that idiom was making a claim about his place while living in comfort behind it. The glazed symmetrical range is the second half of the record and it belongs to a different century from the ditch. Keeping a form because it is cheaper to build or because a mason knows no other is to mistake a habit for a meaning.
questions.hint: Ask who can now take such a castle, and then ask what a visitor in the sixteenth century would have understood the towers to say.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The drum as eye-level and as base
questions.learningObjective: distinguish the visual and structural work of a drum
questions.stem: A dome rests on a tall drum pierced with windows, above a bay carried on four great piers. First say what the drum does for anyone standing in the room, and then say what it does for the shell above it.

options.text: It lifts the springing so the whole underside of the dome is visible from the floor, and it gives the shell the continuous circular base it needs
It hides the springing so the dome appears to float free of the walls, and it reduces the load the four piers have to carry
options.misconception: conceals the springing and claims a load reduction, both of which the drum does not do

options.text: It brings the windows close to the floor so the room is lit from above, and it replaces the pendentives with a simpler construction
options.misconception: moves the windows down and credits the drum with solving the square-to-circle problem

options.text: It raises the dome so the roof clears the piers, and it makes the ring of the base light enough to need no ties
options.misconception: gives the drum a lightness it cannot have, since a base ring needs mass

questions.explanation: Two distinct jobs, and the first is about seeing. A dome that springs from a low ring begins its curve inside the room, so a person below sees only the part of the shell nearest the wall and loses the whole of the far side to perspective; the interior reads as a lid. Raise the springing on a drum and the entire concave surface lifts into the field of view at once, and the windows in the drum admit the light that makes it legible. The second job is structural and is the reason the drum is thick. A dome is generated by rotation and needs a circle to sit on, and a continuous ring of masonry spreads the shell's load along its whole length so that four piers each take a share. A drum cannot be thin and cannot be light, and the windows in it are set deep for that reason. The pendentive problem is solved below the drum, not by it.
questions.hint: Ask what a person below can see when the curve starts low, and what shape the shell needs to stand on.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a grid fixes before a boulevard can be drawn
questions.learningObjective: sequence the planning decisions that precede an avenue
questions.stem: A new avenue is to be cut through a town already laid out on a regular grid. First say what the grid has already fixed, and then say what cutting the avenue through it changes.

options.text: The grid has fixed the scale of the blocks and the direction of the streets, and the avenue overrides one line of it to make a longer axis and a place at its end
The grid has fixed the ownership of every plot, and the avenue is a consequence of the plot boundaries rather than a decision about movement
options.misconception: treats a survey geometry as a property record

options.text: The grid has fixed the level of the ground, and the avenue is only possible because the ground is level along its whole length
options.misconception: reduces the grid to a topographic fact and overlooks the decision

options.text: The grid has fixed the size of the town, and the avenue simply extends the town outward along the line it follows
options.misconception: claims the grid fixes the town's extent, which is what the avenue revises

questions.explanation: The order of the two decisions is the whole argument, and a grid is a statement about scale. Once streets are set out at regular intervals, the size of the block is settled, which settles how deep a building can be and where its light comes from, and the direction of every street is settled too, so nothing in the town can be turned without destroying the pattern. That is the constraint an avenue inherits: it has to run with or against the grain, and if it runs across the grain it has to erase part of the grid to do it. What the cut then produces is a longer line than the grid can generate, a break in the block pattern that is read as a special place, and at the far end the need for a terminus, which is what the square is. The avenue is therefore an exception made inside a system, and the reason it reads as important is precisely that it spends the grid to do it.
questions.hint: Ask what a regular spacing of streets settles about the size of a building plot, and then ask what a line that ignores the grid must break.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The order of building a masonry arch
questions.learningObjective: sequence the stages of constructing a stone arch
questions.stem: A semicircular arch is to be built in masonry over an opening. Put these five stages into the order in which they must be performed.

options.text: Strike the centring so that the arch is left carrying its own weight and nothing else
Cut the voussoirs and set them symmetrically from both springings, working up towards the crown
Set out the opening on its supports and build the timber centring that will carry the ring until it closes
Place the keystone at the crown, which closes the ring and lets the whole arch begin to work
Fill the spandrels and build the wall above over the completed arch, before any support is taken away

questions.explanation: The order is forced by one fact: until the ring is closed, the stones are a loose pile of wedges that will fall. So everything needed to hold them has to exist first, which is what the centring is, a timber falsework built to the exact curve of the arch so the voussoirs can be laid on something. The stones then go in symmetrically from both springings, because building one side higher than the other unbalances the falsework and cracks it, and the symmetry is not aesthetic. The keystone is the last stone of the ring and the one that locks it, so nothing can happen beyond it. The spandrels and the wall above come after the arch is closed but before the support is removed, since that masonry is the load the arch was built to carry and it should be in place when the centring is struck. Only then does the arch hold itself up, and the striking is a test rather than a formality.
questions.hint: Ask what holds the loose stones up before the ring closes, and when the load above should be added.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The order of building a stone vault
questions.learningObjective: sequence the stages of constructing a masonry vault
questions.stem: A stone vault is to be built over a square bay carried on four piers. Put these four stages into the order in which they must be performed.

options.text: Lay the webbing and the severies, the wedge-shaped pieces that form the visible surface of the vault
Set out the bay on the four supports and build the mould or the permanent ribs that will give the vault its curve
Fill the cells above the vault with rubble, keeping as much of the load as possible down near the springings
Strike the support and read the finished curve, checking that the vault is carrying itself in the intended shape

questions.explanation: A vault is a curved surface, and a curve cannot be laid on nothing, so the geometry comes first: the bay is set out on its four supports and either a permanent rib or a timber mould is built to the intended curve, and every later stone is cut to fit that surface. The severies follow, laid symmetrically from the crown outward so that the two halves of the vault are always balanced, which is what keeps the mould from being pushed out of shape. Then the cells are filled. This stage is not tidying, because where the rubble sits changes where the load sits: a vault loaded with heavy material at the crown pushes hardest at the springings, exactly where the masonry has to resist a sideways push, so the fill is kept high and light and the mass is brought down towards the corners. The support comes out last, and its removal is the moment the vault takes its own weight.
questions.hint: Ask what a curve has to be laid on, and where the weight of a vault does the most damage.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The order of investigating scour at a pier
questions.learningObjective: sequence the steps of a structural investigation in a river
questions.stem: A stone bridge pier is reported to be sitting lower than it was. Put these five steps into the order in which they must be performed.

options.text: Take soundings across the flow, upstream of, beside and behind the pier, to measure the hole the report describes
Re-survey the same cross-sections after the next flood, to find out whether the hole is growing or stable
Record the bed level at low water along the channel, since the hole is only measurable when the water drops
Work out where the flow is forced to accelerate and how the bed behind the pier is scoured out
Specify the remedy on the measured figures, such as a cutwater, bed protection or a deeper foundation

questions.explanation: An investigation has to observe before it measures, and it has to measure before it explains. The bed level can only be established at low water, because a sounding taken through moving water confounds the depth of the bed with the state of the river, so the first step is a condition of visibility rather than a piece of theory. The soundings then come, and they have to be taken across the flow rather than on one line, because the object of the exercise is the shape of the hole: upstream, beside, immediately behind, and out in the channel where the bed should be normal. Only then does the mechanism follow, since the readings have to be read against where the flow is forced to accelerate. The remedy is then chosen on the numbers, because a cutwater, a mattress of stone and a deeper foundation are three different answers to three different measurements. The re-survey comes last, since a scour hole that is growing is a different engineering problem from one that has stopped.
questions.hint: Ask what has to be true of the river before a sounding means anything, and what the reading has to be compared with.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The order of laying out a boulevard
questions.learningObjective: sequence the works required before a new avenue is finished
questions.stem: A new avenue is to be built across an existing town. Put these four stages into the order in which they must be performed.

options.text: Pave the carriageway and the footways, then plant and light the street
Set out the axis and the width of the avenue on the ground and fix its levels for the whole length
Excavate the way and lay the sewers and drains, since the water has to be led away before any surface exists
Build the frontages behind the fixed line, to the height and cornice level agreed for the whole avenue

questions.explanation: The first stage is a decision, and nothing can be built until it is made. Setting out the axis fixes a straight line over a kilometre, which is only possible by survey, and fixing the levels at the same time settles how the street will shed its water and where every kerb and threshold must sit; a street whose levels are left to the builders is a street that ponds in the first rain. The underground follows, because drainage is the one part of the work that cannot be added afterwards without digging the street open again, and the gradients set out on the ground are what the sewers are laid to. The frontages come next, built behind a line already fixed, which is what makes a continuous street wall possible: the constraint precedes the building rather than following it. The surface is laid last, after the heavy traffic of construction has finished, because paving put down earlier is paving that has to be relaid.
questions.hint: Ask what has to be decided on the ground before a shovel is used, and which work cannot be undone later.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why thrust dictates the form of an arch
questions.learningObjective: explain how lateral thrust determines arch proportion and buttressing
questions.stem: Explain why the sideways push of an arch governs the shape of the opening and the mass of the wall beside it, and why this is more useful than describing an arch by its span.

answer.exemplar: Begin with the property masonry has and the property it does not. Stone resists being crushed and cannot resist being pulled apart, so every arrangement of it is a search for a way to keep every force in compression. The arch is the answer, and the cost of the answer is the important part. The weight of the wall above a curved opening does not travel down; it travels round the curve and arrives at the springing pointing sideways. That is a real, horizontal, outward push at each side of the opening, and it has to be taken by something. The usual something is a buttress, and the usual lesson is that the buttress is not decoration and not merely support for the wall above, it is the other half of the arch. Once that is granted, the form of the opening is no longer free. A wide opening means a long thrust and a flat curve, so a large mass is needed beside it, and the shape that balances a big thrust economically is a segmental or pointed curve, which directs more of the force downwards and less sideways. A narrow opening in a tall wall can take a semicircle, because the mass is already there. So the proportion of the arch, its rise, its curve, and the number and size of the buttresses are one decision, not four, and they are decided by what has to be held up above and what can be found to hold it out. Consider what a span figure conceals. A span of ten metres means nothing on its own: the same span with a rise of three metres pushes hard outwards, the same span with a rise of eight pushes almost straight down, and the same span in a buttressed wall is a different structure from the same span in a wall with nothing beside it. Span is a measurement; thrust is the argument. A useful answer, then, holds two points together. First, geometry is what makes the arch possible at all, and the profile of the curve is what makes one proportion of arch cheaper than another. Second, the builder's real problem was never the opening but the two forces arriving at its feet, and most of the masonry in sight exists to answer them.

questions.explanation: A full answer starts from the fact that masonry works in compression, follows the load round the curve to the springing, and then argues that the arch's shape and the buttressing are one decision made at the springings. A weak response reports the span and the rise as measurements and never reaches the thrust.
questions.hint: Ask where the weight of the wall above the opening actually arrives, and what stands there to take it.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why a metal frame had to be hidden
questions.learningObjective: explain how a frame made height possible and then had to be protected
questions.stem: Explain how a metal frame made a building far taller than anything in masonry, and why the same frame then had to be enclosed in materials that did no structural work at all.

answer.exemplar: The enabling property is tension, and it is worth being precise about it. A masonry wall carries load by being deep: it is strong while it is being squashed, and it is made strong against being squashed by thickness, so every storey added on top makes the storeys below heavier and the foundations harder. A horizontal member of stone has the same problem in a smaller span, since it must be deep enough to avoid snapping in bending, and a deep member is a heavy one. A frame of metal changes the calculation because the places where its members meet can be made to take a pull as well as a push. When the wind blows, one face of a building is pushed and the opposite face is pulled, and a frame whose joints work in tension behaves as a single cage rather than as a stack of independent members. That is why the members can be slender, and why the limit on height moves from the weight of the wall to the foundations and the wind. The second half of the story is fire, and it is not a minor qualification. Timber does not burn so easily as it looks: its surface chars, the charred layer is an insulator, and the section of the member that is still sound keeps carrying while the surface is consumed. Metal does not behave that way. It conducts, it heats, and it loses strength long before it melts, so heat travels along the frame and turns a local fire into a building-wide one, with the floors still in place and no longer held up. The resolution follows the diagnosis exactly: enclose the frame in a material that does char, whether brick, tile or boarded and plastered work, and let that enclosure take the fire while the frame takes the load. So the same wall that looks like a heavier version of a masonry wall is doing no structural work at all. It is a fire envelope. The building is tall because of the metal and survives because of the masonry, and the two systems are doing opposite jobs, which is why the period's buildings look massive while they are internally hollow.

questions.explanation: A full answer explains the height from tension at the joints, then the fire risk from the failure of metal to char, and connects both to the decision to enclose the frame. A weak response says only that steel is stronger than stone.
questions.hint: Ask what the wind does to the two faces of a tall building, and how a metal member behaves in fire compared with a wooden one.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Grid and avenue as one system
questions.learningObjective: explain how a grid and an avenue together make a city legible
questions.stem: Explain how a regular street grid and a wide avenue made out of it work as one system, and what the avenue can and cannot do inside the grid.

answer.exemplar: Start with what a grid actually is: a decision, taken with a measuring instrument, about how large a piece of ground is and in which direction things run. Set streets at regular intervals and the scale of everything else follows without anybody deciding it separately. Plots become a fixed size, buildings are built to the depth a plot can take, light and air are guaranteed by rule rather than by luck, and the price of land is legible because the unit is legible. A city laid out this way can be described, addressed, taxed and extended by people who were never on the site, and that is the real achievement: geometry converts a settlement into a system. Now the avenue, and it has to be read as a deliberate exception inside that system. The grid produces many short streets; the grid cannot by itself produce a long sightline, a wide surface, or a place with enough room in it for a crowd, because every line it makes is broken again by the next cross street. The avenue overrides part of the pattern to obtain those three things, which is why it costs what it costs. Buildings on both sides that are set to one line and one cornice level turn the space into a street rather than a corridor, and the trees, lamps and paving give the ground a texture the grid never had. Then say what the avenue cannot do, since this is where the account is usually overstated. It cannot make a place in the ordinary sense, because movement is still its first purpose and the crowd it attracts is subordinate to the traffic it carries. It cannot resolve the depth of the blocks on either side, which the grid already fixed and which the avenue has no power over. It cannot make the town walkable, and in the period when these avenues were cut it often made the town less walkable, since the new traffic destroyed the small frontages and the everyday commerce of the old streets. And the two systems are not equally democratic: the grid distributes access widely while the avenue concentrates it, and concentrates it along one line that can be extended, redirected or withdrawn by whoever controls it. The honest conclusion is that the grid is the city and the avenue is an argument made inside it.

questions.explanation: A full answer sets out what the grid fixes, then treats the avenue as a costly exception that supplies sightline, width and a terminus, and closes with the limits of what the avenue can achieve. A weak response describes both as tidiness.
questions.hint: Ask what a repeated interval settles about plot size, and what a grid cannot produce at any width.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the height of a tower claims
questions.learningObjective: explain a tower's height as a social and political statement
questions.stem: Explain what a tower's height claims about the community that built it, and why the height keeps making the claim long after the original reason has gone.

answer.exemplar: Begin with the fact that height is expensive and that expense is only undertaken for a reason. A tower is a very poor way to live and a very poor way to store anything. It is worth building when the thing it does cannot be done at ground level, and that has always meant one of three things: it must be seen, it must be heard, or it must be reached quickly. Seen covers the watch tower on a wall, the signal tower on a coast, and the modern lattice tower that must be identifiable on the horizon for a specific technical reason. Heard covers the bell tower, where the point is not that the bell is high but that the sound is released into open air and travels over the roofs. Reached covers the tower of a church in a crowded town, where height is a way of being above the crowd rather than a way of being tall. In every case the claim is comparative: the tower says that this community can build at a scale that its neighbours cannot, and that whoever stands in it sees or is heard further than they do. Height is a statement about resources and about ambition, and it is made visible to people who will never go up it, which is why it is put where it can be seen from far away. Now the second half, which is the more interesting one. The reason for a tower is nearly always temporary, because the reason stops being true: the watch is replaced, the coast is annexed, the bell is recast, the town expands and the tower that dominated it is now in the middle of something. Yet the tower remains, and it keeps working, because by then it means something other than what it was built to do. It has become a landmark, a navigational mark, a shorthand for the city in a document or a map, an object of local pride, and in most cases a ruin that is still defended precisely because it is a ruin. The persistence is the evidence for the claim: a thing built as a signal and kept as a symbol has told us that the community valued being seen more than it valued what the tower was made to do. It is worth resisting the temptation to call this a function. A tower's height never explains why a city built it and never explains why it kept it.

questions.explanation: A full answer sets out the three reasons a tower is built, then argues that its later survival as a landmark shows the height became a claim in itself. A weak response reduces the tower to its engineering purpose and ignores the social statement.
questions.hint: Ask what a tower can do that a building at ground level cannot, and then ask why one is still standing after that stops being true.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Rise of a semicircular arch
questions.learningObjective: compute the rise of a semicircular arch from its span
questions.stem: A semicircular masonry arch spans an opening of 8 metres between its two springings. How far above the springing line does the crown of the arch stand, in metres?
questions.explanation: In a semicircular arch the curve is half of a full circle and the springing line is the diameter, so the rise from the springing to the crown is the radius, which is half the span. The span is 8 metres, so the radius is 8 divided by 2, which is 4 metres. The second route gives the same figure: a circle's diameter equals twice its radius, so 4 times 2 is 8, which is the span the arch was given. The number is worth more than the arithmetic because it sets the mass of the wall that has to stand beside the opening. A 4-metre rise means the arch pushes hard sideways at its feet, and that is the reason such an opening needs a heavy buttress on each side and a thick wall above, since the weight of that wall is what the arch was built to carry. A flatter arch over the same 8-metre span would rise less and push out more; a taller one would rise more and push out less.
questions.hint: Remember that in a semicircular arch the springing line is the diameter of the full circle.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Bays in an arcade of repeated arches
questions.learningObjective: compute the number of bays in a repeated arcade
questions.stem: An arcade of semicircular arches runs the whole length of a 45 metre wall, every arch spanning 3 metres from the face of one pier to the face of the next. How many arches does the arcade contain?
questions.explanation: The arcade is divided into equal bays and each bay is one arch, so the count is the total length divided by the span of one arch. Here that is 45 metres divided by 3 metres, which is 15. The check is the whole length: 15 arches at 3 metres each is 45 metres, so nothing is left over and the arcade ends exactly at the end of the wall. The measurement matters because it is a clear span, the distance between the faces of the piers, and that is the figure a builder works to when setting out the centring for each arch. A pier has a width of its own, so the distance from the centre of one pier to the centre of the next is the clear span plus that width, and getting the two confused is the usual error: it is the clear span, not the centre-to-centre distance, that the arch has to fit inside.
questions.hint: Divide the length of the wall by the clear span of one arch, then multiply back to check.
